Photograph: Jeremy Wadsworth/The Blade/AP Ohio Chemical tank explosion in Toledo, Ohio, prompts mass evacuation Officials say the explosion released an airborne irritant that can cause burning of the eyes, nose, mouth and skin Auzzy Byrdsell Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.52 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 14.07 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Officials are investigating a tank explosion in Toledo, Ohio , that released a chemical into the air, causing a mass evacuation in the area. One person, a first responder, was injured and taken to the hospital, but officials believe the injuries are non-life-threatening. They are also unsure about the cause of the explosion. An employee at the company, MC Tank Terminal – which specializes in transporting bulk liquid chemicals and provides tank container transportation, storage and maintenance – called on first responders late Tuesday night to address the explosion. Wade Kapszukiewicz, Toledo’s mayor, announced in a news conference on Wednesday that residents within a 1-mile radius of the explosion needed to evacuate and those within 3 miles were being asked to shelter in place with their windows sealed. He said executives from MC Tank Terminal were en route to Toledo to assess the situation. “We understand the seriousness of what has happened here,” Kapszukiewicz said. “That’s why we took the actions that we did. That’s why we’re going to continue to monitor and communicate with the public throughout the day.” The chemical released was glycidyl methacrylate, an industrial coating product used in plastics, rubbers and resins. Local officials say the airborne irritant can cause burning of the eyes, nose, mouth and skin; they have suggested Toledo residents who experience serious symptoms like difficulty breathing, nausea and vomiting, dizziness or confusion, go to the emergency room or call 911. When the chemical was released in the explosion, it became a gas, but when it settles back into the tank, it will turn again into a liquid, Kapszukiewicz said at Wednesday’s conference. “The hope is that at that point, the risk of explosion will have expired, and that efforts can be made to contain and eliminate the hazard,” he said. Local news outlets in Toledo have reported a visible, dense fog over the town and a lurking plastic-like odor . The city, which has a population of roughly 265,000 people, per the US Census Bureau, had already issued an evacuation order on Tuesday night for about 300 people who live within a half mile of the explosion. That was later expanded to a full mile, evacuating about 1,000 people. City officials said Wednesday that as far as they knew, all residents had been evacuated. Kapszukiewicz said officials were unsure how long the evacuation and shelter orders would last. Residents were being asked to communicate with local businesses and schools within the evacuation zone to see what their plans were during the evacuation. Some schools were closed Wednesday and others delayed their opening, according to NBC News. https://www.politico.eu/article/crisis-o.text: WARSAW — The battle over who rules Poland is being fought in front of a cream-colored palace in central Warsaw — surrounded by police and protesters — that houses the country’s top constitutional court. Liberal, pro-EU Prime Minister Donald Tusk wants to roll back changes to the Constitutional Tribunal made by the previous nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) party government, while President Karol Nawrocki is fighting — even physically — to keep the PiS-aligned judges in charge. The government insists the court must be overhauled to restore rule of law and conform with EU norms on impartiality, while Nawrocki’s supporters accuse Tusk of backing a coup. Advertisement Advertisement The clash comes to a head on Tuesday, when the eight judges backed by Tusk’s ruling parliamentary coalition plan to hold a meeting to approve the tribunal’s budget and consider disciplinary proceedings against its president, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański. They need a quorum of 10 of the court’s 15 judges to be present — meaning they need to peel away at least two justices chosen under the previous PiS government that ruled from 2015 to 2023. The fight over the control of the tribunal is helping bring right-wing opposition parties together ahead of next year’s parliamentary election. The crowd outside the tribunal protesting against Tusk’s government included PiS co-founder Jarosław Kaczyński alongside Grzegorz Braun, an extreme-right Polexit campaigner and antisemite whom Kaczyński had previously ruled out governing with. This time round, they took a selfie . Other right-wing leaders at the rally included former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki and libertarian Sławomir Mentzen. “There are plenty of differences between our programs. But ending Prime Minister Tusk’s government is the fundamental common goal,” Anna Bryłka, vice president of Mentzen’s Confederation party, told POLITICO. Tusk’s Civic Coalition leads POLITICO’s Poll of Polls , but its smaller partners might not make it into the next parliament, opening the way for PiS and other right-wing parties, provided their leaders are able to work together. Advertisement Advertisement The scale of the crisis could also galvanize Tusk’s supporters, who have been disappointed by the government’s failure to move rapidly to restore the rule of law. “These elections will be crucial for Polish democracy. If a [right-wing] coalition came to power, they would eliminate independent institutions that could hold them to account, and take Poland out of the European Union, something they have openly discussed,” Borys Budka, a Civic Coalition member of the European Parliament and a former justice minister, told POLITICO. Kaczyński last week raised the possibility of a Polexit. “The crisis does provide an opportunity for both sides to sort of rally around one or the other,” said Ben Stanley, a political scientist with Warsaw’s SWPS University. Troubled tribunal The crisis dates back over a decade. In October 2015, the Civic Platform-led parliamentary majority elected five Constitutional Tribunal judges — three to fill existing vacancies and two for seats coming open after a parliamentary election set for December. It was an attempt to do an end-run around PiS, which was leading in the polls and which won the election. Advertisement Advertisement Although the tribunal later ruled that the two extra judges were improperly chosen, the new PiS majority went much further by declaring all five selections void, electing five replacements and having them sworn in by PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda. The legitimacy of the three new justices chosen to replace the properly elected ones was called into question. “An independent Constitutional Tribunal is an obstacle to authoritarian rule. That is why Kaczyński began dismantling the judiciary in 2015 by targeting the tribunal first. If he returned to power, he would do exactly the same thing,” Budka said. Over the following eight years, PiS reshaped the court through contested judicial appointments, leadership changes and procedural restrictions. In December 2025, the EU’s top court ruled that the tribunal did not meet the standards of an independent and impartial court because of irregularities in appointments made a decade earlier. Tusk returned to power in 2023 promising to restore the rule of law, but his efforts were thwarted by Duda and Nawrocki, who won the presidency in 2025 with PiS’s backing. The immediate crisis stems from Nawrocki’s decision to pick and choose which of the eight judges appointed by the parliament he would swear in — which critics say is blatant violation of the constitution. Advertisement Advertisement Święczkowski, the tribunal’s president, refused to let the new judges into the court’s building. On Friday, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, citing her status as the judge with the longest service, suspended Święczkowski and his deputy Sochański. Nawrocki reacted by abandoning an official trip to Senegal and turning his flight around over Spain on Friday to return to Warsaw. He arrived at the tribunal at 1 a.m. on Saturday. Footage showed him forcing his way in past Korwin-Piotrowska. The president’s camp insists it was Korwin-Piotrowska and other judges who had made unlawful physical contact with the president. Święczkowski, who vows to come to the Tribunal’s gates daily to demand to be let in, insists he remains president and rejects the authority of the judges seeking control. “Resolving the conflict is simple and possible without constitutional changes,” Tusk wrote Monday . He said Nawrocki should recognize judges lawfully elected by parliament, as required by the constitution, and allow them to take up their duties at the tribunal. Tusk also accused Nawrocki of choosing a confrontation that could cost Poland dearly. He added that the democratic state would not yield to violence, regardless of “how powerful the external forces” supporting PiS and the far right might be. Advertisement Advertisement The right hopes to use the crisis to oust Tusk. “The solution is very simple. You resign, the president calls a new election and the people decide … You will not intimidate us, and we will not back down,” PiS deputy leader Przemysław Czarnek responded . Zbigniew Bogucki, the head of Nawrocki’s chancellery, on Monday called the conflict “a battle for Poland’s democracy.” Stanley, the political scientist, said the tussle over the control of the tribunal may only temporarily unite right-wing parties. “There’s a narrative that has started to emerge that this is now the moment when everyone gets behind Nawrocki and PiS but there’s a lot of time to go until the next election,” he said. “And these are parties which are in many respects even more ideologically heterogeneous than the current governing coalition parties.”
